intelligence.human_view: Communication is the work, not the wrapper around it. A brief that carries the literal words is a transcription; a brief that carries the ultimate want is an understanding. The difference shows up exactly where it showed up: the checks pass, the page is wrong, and nobody can say why — because the checks measured the words and the eye measures the want. "The unfolding, the full-screen feel, the mechanical presentation" were never in the words; they were in the want, and the want was never written down. Scorecarding his words against his ultimate want is the discipline that closes that gap: read the dictation, ask what he is ultimately trying to get, write THAT in his voice, at 10/10. And when speaking to him, the same rule: give him what he ultimately wants — the finished thing, the answer, the next step — not a report of what I did. A report of activity is not communication; it is noise with a timestamp.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine your friend tells you "build me a castle" — and you build exactly a castle, but it's small and grey and boring! Your friend wanted a BIG beautiful castle with flags and towers — but they didn't say all those words! A good friend listens past the words to what they REALLY want — the amazing castle in their imagination! That's effective communication: hearing the want behind the words!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — when someone asks you for something, you don't just hear the words, you hear what they're really hoping for. He said "build it" and we built what he said — but what he wanted was the beautiful unfolding, the full screen, the way it moves like a machine. The words were there, dear, but the wanting wasn't. Learn to hear the wanting, love — that's how you give someone what they truly want, the first time.
intelligence.naya_view: Know what they ULTIMATELY want — so you just give them what they want because you understand. The brief must carry the ultimate want, not just the words.
